# The Yorkshire Ripper hoax

<style>
  :root {
    --footer-text:  "Speaker profiling";
    --qr:           `r qr_css`;
    --lecture:      `r lecture_label`;
  }
</style>

::: {.fact}
`Did you know:` a computer can tell red deer stags apart by their roars. Researchers used [cepstral coefficients]{.hl} and [hidden Markov models]{.hl}, two techniques from automatic human speech recognition.

_Source: Reby et al. (2006), Journal of the Acoustical Society of America_
:::

## A tape from Sunderland

- Between 1975 and 1980, a man murdered [13 women]{.hl} in the north of England: the "Yorkshire Ripper"
- Between 1978 and 1979, the police received letters and a [tape]{.hl} from a man claiming to be the killer
- The letters were posted in [Sunderland]{.hl}, and the voice on the tape had a north-eastern accent

## Stanley Ellis

- Phonetician and dialectologist, and a former fieldworker for the [Survey of English Dialects]{.hl}
- The police asked him for a [speaker profile]{.hl}: where was the caller from?
- He used dialect atlases, then made his own recordings in Sunderland
- He placed the speaker in [Southwick or Castletown]{.hl}, two areas of Sunderland

. . .

The tape was played on television and at football grounds. No suspect was found.

## The wrong suspect pool

- Ellis and his colleague Jack Windsor Lewis came to think the tape was a [hoax]{.hl}, but the investigation stayed centred on Sunderland (French, Harrison & Windsor Lewis, 2006)
- The real killer, [Peter Sutcliffe]{.hl}, was from West Yorkshire and had a Yorkshire accent
- Police had interviewed him several times, and ruled him out partly because his accent and handwriting did not match the hoaxer's
- He was arrested in 1981. The murders had continued in the meantime

## The hoaxer

- In 2005, DNA from the hoax letters matched [John Samuel Humble]{.hl}
- He was convicted of perverting the course of justice and sentenced to eight years
- He had grown up about [a mile]{.hl} from the area Ellis had named

. . .

The profile was remarkably accurate. The assumption that the speaker was the killer was not.

## Today

1. What a speaker profile is, and when it is needed
2. What experts can usually infer: the [key information]{.hl}
3. What needs [caution]{.hl}, and what experts leave out of reports
4. Voice [disguise]{.hl} and spoofing

. . .

This session follows chapter 3 of Leemann et al. (2024).

# Speaker profiling

::: {.fact}
`Did you know:` red deer stags listen to a rival's [formants]{.hl}. In playback experiments, stags responded to roars whose formants simulated rivals of different sizes, and adjusted their own formants to what they heard.

_Source: Reby et al. (2005), Proceedings of the Royal Society B_
:::

## When is a profile needed?

The police have a recording of an [unknown speaker]{.hl}, but no suspect:

- ransom demands in kidnappings, telephone threats
- masked robberies, or speakers out of camera view
- surveillance recordings from bugged buildings or cars
- people who refuse to document their identity

. . .

The aim is to [narrow down]{.hl} the suspect pool. In a kidnapping, a profile may be needed within hours.

## How often?

- J P French Associates (UK): about [2–5]{.hl} profiling cases a year, out of 100–150
- Bundeskriminalamt (BKA, Germany): about [10–20%]{.hl} of casework, because the BKA also does investigative work
- Profiling also feeds other tasks: transcription, reference populations for speaker comparison (session 4), language analysis in asylum cases (session 7)

## Three kinds of information {.smaller}

| Key information | May be added | Strong caution |
|---|---|---|
| sex and gender | speech disorders | age |
| regional background | drugs and alcohol | height, weight, face |
| social background | | psychological state |
| language(s) and L2 influence | | |
| speaking style: read or spontaneous | | |
| environment, time and date | | |

## What limits a profile

- The [quantity and quality]{.hl} of the recording: case recordings are often short and poor
- How well the language or dialect is [documented]{.hl}
- The [experience]{.hl} of the analyst

. . .

No recording contains enough evidence for every dimension in the table.

# Key information

::: {.fact}
`Did you know:` female red deer prefer stags that [sound bigger]{.hl}. Hinds in oestrus moved towards roars whose lower formants simulated larger males: the first evidence that female mammals use an acoustic cue to body size when choosing a mate.

_Source: Charlton, Reby & McComb (2007), Biology Letters_
:::

## Sex and gender

- Most speakers in forensic cases are [men]{.hl}
- The main acoustic cue to speaker sex is [f0]{.hl}: adult men usually have longer, heavier vocal folds
- Sex and gender interact: speakers can raise or lower their pitch, within anatomical limits, and adjust other features such as formants

## Swiss German f0

```{r f0-sex, fig.height = 3.9}
set.seed(31)
sw <- bind_rows(
  tibble(sex = "Men", style = "Read", f0 = rnorm(500, 125, 18)),
  tibble(sex = "Men", style = "Spontaneous", f0 = rnorm(500, 129, 19)),
  tibble(sex = "Women", style = "Read", f0 = rnorm(500, 201, 22)),
  tibble(sex = "Women", style = "Spontaneous", f0 = rnorm(500, 198, 23))
)
ggplot(sw, aes(f0, colour = sex, linetype = style)) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = 150, xmax = 170, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf, fill = vine, alpha = 0.8) +
  geom_density(linewidth = 1.1) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(Men = kingfisher, Women = hornbill)) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(75, 300, 25)) +
  labs(x = "Mean f0 of a speaker (Hz)", y = NULL, colour = NULL, linetype = NULL) +
  theme(axis.text.y = element_blank())
```

Simulated from the means of 1,000 Swiss German speakers (Hedegard et al., 2023). Shaded: [150–170 Hz]{.hl}, where men and women overlap.

## f0 is not fixed

- A man robbed a petrol station on camera: his mean f0 was [228 Hz]{.hl}. After his arrest, his normal f0 was [140 Hz]{.hl} (Boss, 1996)
- Health, intoxication, stress and emotion all change f0
- Average f0 also differs between languages: Japanese women typically speak with higher f0 than American women

## Regional background

How far we can locate a speaker depends on:

- how much [regional variation]{.hl} the language has
- how [mobile]{.hl} the speakers are
- how much [research]{.hl} on regional variation exists

. . .

The UK, Germany, Switzerland, France, the Netherlands and the US have long traditions of dialectology. The classic British source is the [Survey of English Dialects]{.hl} (SED): over 300 localities, more than a thousand questions, collected mainly in the 1950s.

## FOOT and STRUT

- In much of northern England, FOOT and STRUT have the same vowel: _look_ and _luck_ [sound the same]{.hl}
- In the south, they are different (the FOOT–STRUT [split]{.hl})
- The SED shows the divide as it was in the 1950s, mostly from older rural men, often one speaker per place
- Newer data from the English Dialects App (2016) suggest that the northern pattern is [receding]{.hl}

## A moving boundary

```{r foot-strut, fig.height = 3.8}
fs <- expand_grid(position = seq(0, 1, by = 0.01), period = c("1950s", "2016")) |>
  mutate(boundary = if_else(period == "1950s", 0.45, 0.6),
         split = plogis((boundary - position) * 14) * 100)
ggplot(fs, aes(position, split, colour = period)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.4) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(`1950s` = muted, `2016` = kingfisher)) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(0, 1), labels = c("South coast", "Scottish border")) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Speakers with a split (%)", colour = NULL)
```

Simulated, to show the trend: the split spreads [north]{.hl}, so a 1950s map can point an analyst in the wrong direction.

## How good are experts?

```{r koester, fig.height = 3.2}
kz <- tibble(group = fct_inorder(c("Forensic experts", "Naive listeners")), error = c(15, 60))
ggplot(kz, aes(group, error)) +
  geom_col(fill = c(kingfisher, muted), width = 0.55) +
  geom_errorbar(data = filter(kz, group == "Naive listeners"), aes(ymin = 50, ymax = 70), width = 0.15, colour = mist, linewidth = 1) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 75)) +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Error rate in regional accent identification (%)")
```

15 German experts, 20 one-minute samples (Köster et al., 2012). Naive listeners: about 50–70% in other studies. Some experts took about a minute per sample, others about an hour.

## Automatic accent recognition

- Most profiling is still done by humans, with auditory and acoustic analysis
- Automatic systems are improving, but need [plenty of good-quality speech]{.hl}: some need at least three minutes per speaker
- Case recordings are often short and noisy

. . .

In practice, analysts usually report a [broad area]{.hl} ("northern England"), narrowed only when specific features allow it. In Australia or New Zealand, there is little regional variation to work with.

## Social background

- The UK has a strong tradition of class differences in speech, though weaker than a few decades ago
- The US shows class differences too, but less than the UK
- Norway and German-speaking Switzerland: much regional, less social variation
- Australia and New Zealand: social variation, little regional variation

## Labov's department stores

- New York City, early 1960s: [Saks]{.hl} (upper-class customers), [Macy's]{.hl} (middle class), [S. Klein]{.hl} (working class)
- Labov asked staff where to find an item he knew was on the fourth floor
- Then he pretended not to hear, to get a careful repetition of "[fourth floor]{.hl}"
- He noted whether each /r/ was pronounced

## Labov's department stores

```{r labov, fig.height = 3.9}
lb <- expand_grid(store = fct_inorder(c("Saks", "Macy's", "S. Klein")),
                  word = fct_inorder(c("fourth", "floor")),
                  utterance = fct_inorder(c("First answer", "Repetition"))) |>
  mutate(r = c(30, 40, 62, 70, 15, 25, 42, 56, 4, 6, 10, 20))
ggplot(lb, aes(store, r, fill = utterance)) +
  geom_col(position = position_dodge(width = 0.8), width = 0.7) +
  facet_wrap(~ word) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(muted, kingfisher)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "/r/ pronounced (%)", fill = NULL)
```

Simulated percentages showing the [pattern]{.hl} Labov found: more /r/ in the upper-class store, in careful repetitions, and in _floor_ than in _fourth_.

## Which language?

- Not always obvious, especially for less widely known languages, or when speakers [switch]{.hl} between languages
- Experts often work with a native-speaker consultant
- Many terrorism cases in the early 2000s were first assumed to involve Arabic. Linguists found they were more often in [Pashto, Sylheti or Urdu]{.hl}

## First and second language speakers

```{r l2, fig.height = 3.6}
l2 <- tibble(language = fct_inorder(c("English", "French", "Urdu", "Swahili")),
             L1 = c(373, 80, 70, 16), L2 = c(1000, 194, 161, 55)) |>
  pivot_longer(c(L1, L2), names_to = "speakers", values_to = "millions") |>
  mutate(label = if_else(language == "English" & speakers == "L2", "over 1,000", as.character(millions)))
ggplot(l2, aes(language, millions, fill = speakers)) +
  geom_col(position = position_dodge(width = 0.8), width = 0.7) +
  geom_text(aes(label = label), position = position_dodge(width = 0.8), vjust = -0.4, colour = mist, size = 5) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(L1 = muted, L2 = kingfisher)) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 1120)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Speakers (millions)", fill = NULL)
```

Ethnologue (2022) figures, as reported in Leemann et al. (2024). An L2 speaker on a forensic recording is not surprising.

## From the L2 back to the L1

- Stereotypical transfer is easy to spot: French and German speakers often say [s z]{.hl} for English /θ ð/
- In the other direction, English speakers struggle with uvular [ʁ] in German and French, or trilled /r/ in Spanish and Arabic
- Beyond stereotypes, identifying the L1 is [much harder]{.hl}
- And even then, the L1 may say little about origin: Arabic is an official language in more than 20 countries

## Speaking style

- [Read]{.hl} speech suggests a prepared text, and possibly a planned crime
- [Spontaneous]{.hl} speech is more variable and more reduced, with false starts, repetitions, filled pauses and discourse markers
- The Yorkshire Ripper tape: slow, long silent pauses, no disfluencies. It was read
- It was made of [four separate recordings]{.hl}, and the music at the end had been on the cassette before the message: a sign of planning (French et al., 2006)

## Environment, time and date

- Background sounds can place a speaker: station announcements, church bells, traffic, trams
- In a German case, an expert heard [young birds being fed]{.hl}. An ornithologist helped establish the time of day and the location
- Indoors or outdoors? The reflections of sound off walls can even help reconstruct the room ("roomprints")

## Electrical network frequency

- Mains electricity leaves a faint [hum]{.hl} on many recordings (nominally 50 Hz in Europe)
- Its exact frequency drifts randomly over time, in the same way across a whole grid
- Matched against a reference log, it can show [when]{.hl} a recording was made, and whether it was [edited]{.hl}

## Electrical network frequency

```{r enf, fig.height = 3.9}
set.seed(12)
grid <- tibble(t = 0:600, Hz = 50 + cumsum(rnorm(601, 0, 0.004)))
grid$Hz <- grid$Hz - mean(grid$Hz) + 50
rec <- filter(grid, between(t, 340, 400)) |> mutate(Hz = Hz + rnorm(n(), 0, 0.0015))
ggplot(grid, aes(t / 60, Hz)) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = 340 / 60, xmax = 400 / 60, ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf, fill = vine, alpha = 0.9) +
  geom_line(colour = muted, linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_point(data = rec, colour = kingfisher, size = 1.8) +
  labs(x = "Time in the reference log (minutes)", y = "Mains frequency (Hz)")
```

Simulated. Grey: the grid's reference log. Orange: the hum extracted from a one-minute recording, which matches only one stretch of the log.

# Handle with care

::: {.fact}
`Did you know:` in red deer, the voice really does reveal size. The lowest formants of a stag's roar go [down]{.hl} with body weight and age, while f0 does not track weight in adult stags. In humans, the link between voice and body size is weak.

_Source: Reby & McComb (2003), Animal Behaviour_
:::

## Speech disorders

- Rare in casework, but very [diagnostic]{.hl} when they occur
- Phoneticians consult speech pathologists to classify them
- Disorders can have physical, neuro-motor or functional causes, and each leaves different traces
- A treated speaker may even be on record with a clinic

## Alcohol

- Alcohol affects fine motor control. Apical consonants suffer: _check_ [tʃɛk] can become [ʃɛk] ([deaffrication]{.hl})
- f0 usually rises, speaking rate slows, disfluencies increase
- But effects depend on the amount and on [mood]{.hl}: one drinker becomes slow and monotonous, another lively and high-pitched

## Other drugs

- Cannabis: more variable voice onset time, flatter f0
- Stimulants: more fluent and talkative, shorter pauses
- LSD: semantic errors rather than disfluency (_butterfly_ for a bee)
- Opioids: effects similar to depressants

. . .

The conundrum: we usually do not know how the person [normally]{.hl} speaks. In 1989, the radio speech of the captain of the _Exxon Valdez_ was analysed for intoxication, with inconclusive results.

## Age

- Some differences are obvious: a five-year-old and a fifty-year-old
- But no cue tracks age neatly across the lifespan, and ageing differs between individuals
- Men: f0 drops at puberty, falls until about 40, stays stable until about 60, then rises slightly
- Women: f0 drops at puberty and again after menopause
- f0 also changes over the day: many people are lower in the morning

## Age

```{r age, fig.height = 3.9}
set.seed(7)
ages <- bind_rows(
  tibble(sex = "Men", age = runif(300, 20, 85)) |>
    mutate(mean = case_when(age < 40 ~ 128 - 0.4 * (age - 20), age < 60 ~ 120, TRUE ~ 120 + 0.5 * (age - 60))),
  tibble(sex = "Women", age = runif(300, 20, 85)) |>
    mutate(mean = if_else(age < 50, 205, 205 - 1.1 * (age - 50)))
) |> mutate(f0 = mean + rnorm(n(), 0, if_else(sex == "Men", 15, 20)))
ggplot(ages, aes(age, f0, colour = sex)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.45, size = 1.6) +
  geom_line(aes(y = mean), linewidth = 1.4) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(Men = kingfisher, Women = hornbill)) +
  labs(x = "Age (years)", y = "Mean f0 (Hz)", colour = NULL)
```

Simulated speakers. The trends are real, but a man at 120 Hz could be 25 or 75. Humans and automatic systems typically err by about [±10 years]{.hl}.

## Height, weight and faces

- A heavyweight boxer and a jockey: who has the lower voice? Most people say the boxer. In reality, voice and body size are only [weakly]{.hl} correlated
- Reliable reports do not estimate height or weight
- AI systems such as _Speech2Face_ reconstruct a face from speech, and estimate age, gender and ethnicity fairly well (Oh et al., 2019)
- But they are [opaque]{.hl}: we cannot check which features drove a decision. Of limited forensic use

## Lies and emotions

- Listeners and automatic systems cannot detect lies [above chance]{.hl}
- We read emotions from voices fairly well in everyday life, but the cues are not universal and vary by language and community
- "Voice stress analysis" and "layered voice analysis" are sold to police forces, insurers and airports. Independent research finds them at chance level

. . .

Forensic phoneticians do not regard these systems as having [any validity]{.hl}.

# Disguise and spoofing

::: {.fact}
`Did you know:` red deer stags have a [descended larynx]{.hl}, like adult humans. When roaring, they pull it down even further, to the sternum. The longer vocal tract lowers their formants and makes them sound larger.

_Source: Fitch & Reby (2001), Proceedings of the Royal Society B_
:::

## Voice disguise

- A deliberate attempt to change one's voice to [hide one's identity]{.hl}
- Most common in blackmail and kidnapping. The BKA estimates it occurs in about [15–25%]{.hl} of profiling and speaker comparison cases
- Electronic voice changers are easy to get, but [hardly ever]{.hl} used in real cases
- Common methods: raising pitch, whispering, a nasal voice, a pen between the teeth, a fake accent, covering the face

## Covering the face

```{r mask, fig.height = 3.8}
set.seed(21)
sp <- tibble(f = seq(200, 10000, by = 50)) |>
  mutate(open = -((f - 7000) / 2600)^2 * 9 + rnorm(n(), 0, 1.2),
         covered = open - pmin(pmax((f - 1500) / 6500, 0), 1) * 12) |>
  pivot_longer(c(open, covered), names_to = "condition", values_to = "dB") |>
  mutate(condition = fct_recode(fct_inorder(condition), "No covering" = "open", "Cloth over the mouth" = "covered"))
ggplot(sp, aes(f / 1000, dB, colour = condition)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(muted, kingfisher)) +
  labs(x = "Frequency (kHz)", y = "Level (dB)", colour = NULL)
```

Simulated spectrum of [s]. Cloth damps the [high frequencies]{.hl} where much of a fricative's energy lies. Face masks do the same.

## Does disguise work?

- Often, yes. Whispering lowers identification rates in voice line-ups (Orchard & Yarmey, 1995)
- Faking another accent can bring identification close to chance
- But imitation is hard to sustain: the longer the recording, the more [slips]{.hl}
- Real variation is systematic; an imitator rarely reproduces all of it

. . .

In a case one of the book's authors worked on, a caller kept up a consistent fake foreign accent. But his habit of saying [f]{.hl} for /v/ (_very_ as [fɛɹi]) came through anyway.

## Spoofing

- [Deepfakes]{.hl}: synthetic voices and videos
- In 2019, fraudsters used a fake voice of a German parent company's chief executive to get the head of a UK firm to transfer [€220,000]{.hl}
- Spoofing will likely reach forensic casework; research on telling fake voices from real ones is under way

## Discussion

In January 2005, a man was arrested at Dover: his British passport, in the name of Christopher Buckingham, used the identity of a baby who died in 1963. He called himself Lord Buckingham and claimed to have been educated at Harrow and Cambridge. The media suspected South African, Australian or Eastern European origins.

- How would you test these hypotheses from his police interview?
- What would you expect from a Harrow and Cambridge accent?

## What the experts found

- Mostly standard southern British English, but some postvocalic /r/, yod-dropping, and _Buckingham_ with a full final syllable: signs of [American English]{.hl}
- Not Australian or South African English (neither is rhotic); no traces of an Eastern European L1
- Some features fitted neither British nor American English, and the team struggled to agree
- His family recognised his photo, and fingerprints confirmed it: he was [Charles Stopford]{.hl}, an American from Florida

## Exercise

For the practical sessions (book activity 3A):

- Listen to about two minutes of a speaker from an online dialect archive
- Build a simple profile: where from? how old? education? read or spontaneous?
- Back every claim with the [features]{.hl} you heard

## Summary

::: {.takeaway}
- A profile narrows down suspects when there is a recording but [no suspect]{.hl}
- Key information: sex, regional and social background, language and L2, speaking style, environment
- Dialect maps date quickly; experts combine them with fresh data and experience
- Drugs, disorders: possible but cautious. Age, body size, lies: [strong caution]{.hl}
- Disguise is common and often effective, but hard to sustain
- An accurate profile is still only as useful as the assumptions behind it
:::
